text: Each of the 19 schemas is created by the ACE DBA account in one transaction, owned by the login of the same name, with UTF8 and the server default collation, in the default tablespace, with ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES granted to that login only and search_path set to the service's own schema.
why: The sources fix one schema and one login per service and the 19 names, and fix none of the creation options; the script cannot be written and the environments cannot be compared without one option per attribute.
read: Template and Rules v1 section R4; Architecture v5 slides 29, 39 and 41; Business Requirements Program v4 NFR-053 (encrypted at rest and in transit); no source read gives an encoding, a collation, a tablespace, a default privilege set or a search_path.
applied_in: Section 3 Preconditions, section 4 Flow steps 3 to 5, section 11 Data and section 13 Solution plan
impact: Low: a different encoding, collation or tablespace is a value of the script and changes no acceptance criterion; the ownership rule, the PUBLIC revoke and the closed list hold either way.

text: DEV and SIT receive the 19 schemas in wave 0 by this story, and UAT and PROD receive them by the same idempotent script at the release of the first service of each wave, each run with its own change record and run by the ACE DBA role.
why: Wave 0 names the 19 schemas and logins as a platform item and no source states which environments receive them, which role runs the script or which change record a run needs; the story must state where it is done and cannot hold a production run without a role and a record.
read: Architecture v5 slide 38 (wave 0 platform once, '19 schemas + logins'); slide 29 (one ACE PostgreSQL server); Template and Rules v1 sections R5.6 and R5.7 rule 6; no source read names the wave 0 environment set, the running role or a change record.
applied_in: Section 2 Business rationale, section 3 Preconditions, section 10 Authority and section 13 Solution plan
confirm: ACE DBA, platform administrator and release role
impact: Low: moving a UAT or PROD run earlier or later changes the run sheet and the change record and no criterion; the script is the same in all four environments because the 19 names are fixed literals.

text: The legacy NF-06 story text is absent from the source set, so the story is written from Arch v5 slides 11, 29, 38, 39 and 41 and from Template and Rules section R4, its seven criteria are new under D-RCV-60, and they stand in for the legacy criteria and test cases until the legacy file is supplied.
why: The legacy index entry for NF-06 holds the title and zero characters, with no story file and no criteria, test cases, messages or sections, so nothing can be copied word for word although the disposition is Moved (no impact).
read: _work/msr/plan/legacy_index.json entry NF-06 (title only, chars 0, story_file null); Template and Rules v1 section R3 (source precedence) and section R9; Architecture v5 slides 11, 29, 38, 39 and 41.
applied_in: Section 1 Story, section 3 Preconditions, section 7 Acceptance criteria, section 16 Test cases and section 19 Out of scope
impact: If the NF-06 text is later published and contradicts a criterion, AC1 to AC7 are restated against it and the test cases follow; the deliverable, the closed list and the boundary assertion do not change.

text: The login owns its schema, the migrations of that schema are applied by the per-service migrator login of RWB-PLT-N011-DB, and this story grants no DDL beyond the ownership that CREATE SCHEMA AUTHORIZATION gives.
why: Slide 29 states that the login owns its schema and that each service runs its own Flyway migrations, and no source names a migrator login or says that the owning login applies the migrations itself; a statement of the split is needed so that a build team knows which identity its migrations run as.
read: Architecture v5 slide 29 rules text; slide 39 decision 2; Template and Rules v1 section R5.5 DP-15; WP B-PLT-DB-01, which lists RWB-PLT-N011-DB as 'PgBouncer pools, migrator role and grant check'.
applied_in: Section 3 Preconditions, section 10 Authority and section 13 Solution plan (ordering note)
impact: A reversal changes no criterion of this story: the ownership and the refusals stay, and only the identity that runs a migration changes in the service DB stories.

text: Until the ACE DBA names them, each pool runs in transaction pooling mode with one entry per service login, a statement timeout of 5 s from Arch v5 slide 11, an initial connection cap and pool size per login that the ACE DBA sets before the first release, and every number held as a configuration value and never in code; the platform does not substitute a default for a missing per-login cap.
why: Arch v5 fixes one pool per login with a connection cap and a statement timeout and gives a single number, the 5 s statement timeout of the SQL view standard; no source gives the pool mode, the pool size, the cap, the idle and connection timeouts or the server-side reserve, and the story cannot be configured or tested without one shape.
read: Read as a protection shape that changes no business behaviour and no contract: it adds one entry per login and no shared entry, it keeps the 5 s timeout of the standard, and every cap stays a configuration value that the ACE DBA may change without a code change.
applied_in: Section 3 Preconditions; section 11 Data (the 19 pools); section 13 Solution plan
confirm: ACE DBA and solution architect confirm the pool mode, the pool size, the cap per login and the timeouts before the first release.
impact: Low: a different mode or a different cap is a configuration change and no acceptance criterion changes; a cap left unset is still a failed build, because AC5 refuses a pool without a cap.

text: There is one migrator login per service, named after its schema with the suffix _migrator (rwb_case_migrator for schema rwb_case), it owns nothing, it is a member of no service login, it holds DDL on its own schema only and no right on any other rwb_* schema, on public or on recovery, and it is created once per service by the ACE DBA with its credential held in the key store and reached by a reference.
why: Arch v5 states one owning login per service and one Flyway sequence per service and never names the account that applies the migrations; the story needs a migrator identity to state the own-schema-only rule of AC3 and the attribute rule of AC4, and the naming has to be fixed for the 19 logins to be configured and checked.
read: Read as the smallest identity that satisfies the slide 29 rules without widening one: the service login keeps ownership and the application grant, the migrator login gains DDL inside one schema and nothing else, and the check refuses any right outside it.
applied_in: Section 3 Preconditions; section 11 Data (the 19 migrator logins); section 13 Solution plan
confirm: ACE DBA and solution architect confirm the migrator login naming, its privilege list and the credential path before the first release.
impact: Low: a different suffix or a different privilege list is a rename or a grant change in one migration and no acceptance criterion changes; a shared migrator across services would break AC3 and is refused by the check.

text: Until the sources name the product, the platform runs PgBouncer itself in front of the ACE PostgreSQL server, with one database or user entry per service login so that the connection cap and the statement timeout are per login and the pool counters are readable on the platform metrics path, and the deployment shape is confirmed by the ACE DBA before wave 1.
why: Arch v5 names PgBouncer and the managed Azure Database for PostgreSQL server and no product shape; a per-login cap, a per-login statement timeout and a readable counter set are all easier to guarantee and to test when the platform owns the pool process.
read: Read from Arch v5 slide 29 as the mechanism the architecture already chose and from NFR-020 and NFR-021 as the reason a per-login cap exists; the choice adds no business behaviour and no contract.
applied_in: Section 3 Preconditions; section 4 Flow step 2; section 11 Data; section 13 Solution plan
confirm: Platform template owner, ACE DBA and solution architect confirm the product and the deployment shape before wave 1.
impact: Low: the managed feature would move the configuration into the database service and change where the counters come from, while the 19 caps, the 5 s timeout and the check stay the same.

text: Until the DevOps lead fixes it, the grant check is one blocking stage of the platform pipeline that runs beside the migration lint and the drift gate of RWB-PLT-E1044-CON, publishes one result per login per run attached to the run, and is kept with the pipeline history for the audit period agreed with internal audit.
why: Arch v5 requires a check in every build and NFR-054 requires the pipeline to block, and no source says which pipeline runs it, what it publishes or how long the result is kept; the story cannot be wired or audited without one shape.
read: Read as the minimum that satisfies both sources: the stage is blocking, it sits beside the RWB-PLT-E1044-CON stages and never inside them, and it publishes a per-login result that an audit role can read after the run.
applied_in: Section 4 Flow steps 6 and 7; section 5 Exception paths; section 13 Solution plan; section 14 Validation and messages
confirm: DevOps lead and the platform administrator confirm the stage, its published result and the retention with the audit role.
impact: Low: a result written to another store or a longer retention changes the stage configuration and no acceptance criterion; a non-blocking stage would break AC5 and is refused.
